newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia posts trade surplus, prices in check.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia posts trade surplus, prices in check.

text.p: Indonesia posted a healthy trade surplus in 1996 and inflation remains in check, but officials and economists said on Wednesday it will have to ensure overheating does not occur.

"I think our economy is on the right track. Inflation is under control and we will work further to get it down to five percent as targeted," Coordinating Minister for Economics, Finance and Supervisor of Development Saleh Afiff told Reuters.
Information Minister Harmoko said earlier that Indonesia's consumer price index rose 1.05 percent month-on-month in February, compared with a rise of 1.03 percent in January.
Year-on-year inflation in February was 4.68 percent, compared with 5.34 percent in January.
Harmoko also said Indonesia posted a trade surplus of $6,946.3 million in 1996 against $4,754.6 million in 1995. Total exports were $49.81 billion against imports of $42.87 billion.
"The trade surplus itself for 1996 is positive. The fall in non-oil export growth has been offset by strong oil export earnings," Sim Moh Siong, an economist at Citibank, told Reuters.
Sim said Indonesia's inflation figures were positive.
"Indonesia has been experiencing a steady fall in inflation which has allowed the central bank to lower interest rates. But I think the engine of the economy is still running strong."
"This is being reflected in a pick-up in import growth which makes the improvement in trade unlikely to persist," Sim said.
"Furthermore the money supply and loan growth are still running strong. There is now little scope for lower interest rates," the economist said.
Broad money supply M2 growth was 29.64 percent year-on-year in December against the government's target of 17 percent for the 1996/97 (April-March) budget. M1 growth was 21.66 percent in December.
Loans grew almost 30 percent year-on-year in December against an initial target of 16 percent for the 1996/97 budget.
"In fact, interest rates may have to be tightened back in order to curb the strong economy from fuelling inflationary pressures," Sim said.

Afiff said the strengthening of oil prices had helped Indonesia earn more money from oil exports, while the strong dollar against the yen helped lower its foreign debt, which is 40-percent denominated in yen.
"Our foreign debts are manageable," Afiff said. The World Bank has estimated the country's foreign debt at $100 billion.
Indonesian Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said on Tuesday the country's 1996/97 (April-March) budget will have a surplus of 817.9 billion rupiah.
He told a parliamentary hearing the 1996/97 budget revenue would be at 95.840 trillion rupiah and spending at 95.022 trillion.
Mar'ie also predicted the price of crude oil would be an average $20.76 per barrel during the fiscal year ending March 31 against the targeted price of $16.50 per barrel.
OPEC member Indonesia currently produces around 1.58 million barrels of crude oil and condensate.
